compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: Mixed workload: tiny 16x32 matmuls per window (compute-light), large number of windows (57600), heavy global memory traffic for weights and activations.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.risk: Tiny matmul sizes may not saturate tensor cores; kernel launch overhead if not persistent.

memory_bandwidth.notes: Input: 1×720×1280×32 fp16 = ~59MB. Weights: qkv(32×96), proj(32×32), fc1(32×128), fc2(128×32) = small. RPE bias: 1×1×16×16 fp16 = tiny. Total read/write dominated by activation tensors. Reference does multiple kernel launches reading/writing activations repeatedly. Fused kernel reads input once, writes output once, reads weights from L2/shared.

register_pressure.notes: Per window: 16 tokens × 32 dims = 512 fp16 values = 256 fp32 values for accumulation. Plus QKV intermediates (3×512), attn matrix (16×16=256), MLP intermediates (16×128=2048). Total registers very high if all kept in registers.
register_pressure.risk: Very high register pressure for fully persistent single-kernel approach; may need to spill or use shared memory for MLP intermediates.

nodes.notes:
ANALYSIS:
1) Problem classification: Fused transformer block kernel. Mixed: LayerNorm (reduction over dim=32), QKV projection (small matmul 16×32 × 32×96), attention (16×16 softmax + 16×32 matmul), output projection, residual, second LayerNorm, MLP up-projection (16×32 × 32×128), GELU, MLP down-projection (16×128 × 128×32), residual. All per-window (16 tokens, dim=32). 57600 independent windows (1×180×320 windows of 4×4). Primary output: B×H×W×C tensor. Reductions: LayerNorm over C=32, softmax over N=16, matmuls.
2) Canonical math: For each window w: x_w = input[w] (16×32 fp16). ln1 = LayerNorm(x_w). qkv = ln1 @ W_qkv + b_qkv (16×96). q,k,v = split(qkv). attn = softmax(q*scale @ k^T + rpe_bias) (16×16). o = attn @ v (16×32). proj = o @ W_proj + b_proj (16×32). r1 = x_w + proj. ln2 = LayerNorm(r1). up = GELU(ln2 @ W_fc1 + b_fc1) (16×128). down = up @ W_fc2 + b_fc2 (16×32). output = r1 + down.
3) Data layout: Input (1,720,1280,32) fp16 contiguous NHWC. Weights small, broadcast across all windows. RPE bias (1,1,16,16) fp16. All dense access. Window partition is a reshape+permute but with stride tricks can be computed via index arithmetic.
4) Bottleneck regimes: (a) Bandwidth-bound: if kernel is well-fused, dominated by reading 59MB input + writing 59MB output ≈ 118MB at 1.8TB/s → ~65μs lower bound. (b) Compute-bound: 57600 windows × (16×32×96 + 16×16×32 + 16×32×32 + 16×32×128 + 16×128×32) × 2 FLOPs ≈ 57600 × (98304+16384+16384+131072+131072) = 57600 × 393216 ≈ 22.6 GFLOP. At ~660 TFLOP/s fp16 tensor core → ~34μs. So roughly balanced. (c) Latency-bound: if too many small kernels launched sequentially (reference path). (d) Register-pressure-bound: if persistent kernel spills heavily.
5) Kernel design space knobs: (i) Parallelization: one program per window vs multiple windows per program vs tiling windows into blocks. (ii) Tiling: tile over C=32 (fits in registers) vs tile over N=16 (small). (iii) Memory: weights in shared memory vs registers vs rely on L2. (iv) Compute: use tl.dot for matmuls vs manual outer products. (v) Numerics: fp16 inputs to tl.dot with fp32 accumulators (required). (vi) Special: GELU via tanh approximation using tl.libdevice.tanh.
6) Skeleton: Phase 1: Load 16×32 tile from global. Phase 2: LN1 in registers (reduce over 32). Phase 3: QKV matmul via tl.dot (load weight columns from shared/global). Phase 4: Attention: scale q, q@k^T via tl.dot, add RPE, online softmax, attn@v via tl.dot. Phase 5: Out proj via tl.dot, add residual. Phase 6: LN2. Phase 7: FC1 via tl.dot + GELU. Phase 8: FC2 via tl.dot + residual. Phase 9: Store output.
7) Candidate families: See child nodes.

action.description: Implement a single Triton kernel where each program handles one 4×4 window (16 tokens × dim=32). The entire block computation (LN1→QKV→Attn→Proj→Res→LN2→MLP→Res) is done without returning to global memory. Weights are loaded from global (hitting L2 cache since they're small and reused across 57600 programs). All intermediate activations live in registers. Use tl.dot for all matmuls with fp16 inputs and fp32 accumulators. Grid = 57600 programs. Start with a straightforward implementation without micro-optimizations.
action.rationale: The reference launches ~10+ separate CUDA kernels (2 LN, 4 linear, 1 softmax, attention matmuls, GELU, residuals). Fusing everything into one kernel eliminates all intermediate global memory traffic (~5× reduction in memory movement) and kernel launch overhead. The main challenge is register pressure (16×128 MLP intermediate = 2048 values), but dim=32 and hidden=128 are small enough that with careful tiling the MLP matmul can be done in tiles.
action.title: Fully-fused single persistent kernel (one program per window)

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: 16×32 matmuls are very small for tensor cores (need BLOCK_M>=16, BLOCK_K>=16). tl.dot requires power-of-2 dims.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: Small matmuls (16x32 x 32x32) don't saturate tensor cores well. allow_tf32=False leaves perf on table.

memory_bandwidth.notes: Eliminated all intermediate global memory traffic. Only read input and write output once.

register_pressure.notes: N=16, C=32 means residuals are 512 fp16 values. MLP tiled at TILE_H=32 keeps intermediate small. Could be tighter.

action.description: Split into 2-3 fused kernels: (1) Fused LN1+QKV+Attention+Proj+Residual kernel, (2) Fused LN2+FC1+GELU+FC2+Residual kernel. Each kernel is simpler to implement and has lower register pressure. The attention kernel handles the complex softmax+matmul logic. The MLP kernel handles the large hidden dimension. Both kernels read/write the activation tensor (one extra round-trip to global memory compared to fully-fused).
action.rationale: Reduces complexity and register pressure compared to fully-fused. Still eliminates most intermediate global memory traffic (only one extra read/write of the activation between the two kernels). Easier to debug and tune. The MLP kernel can use shared memory for the large hidden dim intermediates.

action.description: Implement custom Triton kernels for individual bottleneck operators (fused LN+Linear, fused attention with window partition baked in, fused LN+MLP) while keeping the overall forward() as a sequence of kernel calls. Focus on eliminating the window partition/reverse reshape overhead and fusing adjacent elementwise ops (residual add, GELU). Use torch.mm for the large linear projections where cuBLAS is efficient.
action.rationale: Lowest implementation risk. Each kernel is simple to verify. Main gains come from fusing elementwise ops and eliminating reshape/permute materialization. Limited speedup because multiple kernel launches and intermediate memory traffic remain.

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.risk: Window partition reshape overhead may negate gains; batched GEMM setup cost.

kernel_summary: Simplified single-head Swin Transformer block in FP16 on a 1×720×1280×32 input with 4×4 windows (no shift), producing 57600 independent windows of 16 tokens × dim=32. The block performs: LN1 → QKV projection (32→96) → single-head attention with 16×16 RPE bias + softmax → output projection (32→32) → residual → LN2 → MLP up (32→128) + GELU → MLP down (128→32) → residual. The workload is a mix of small per-window matmuls (compute ~22.6 GFLOP) and activation memory traffic (~59MB input/output). With ~1.8TB/s bandwidth and ~660 TFLOP/s FP16 on RTX5090, the kernel is roughly balanced between compute and bandwidth. The reference implementation launches 10+ CUDA kernels with multiple intermediate buffer materializations. The key optimization opportunity is fusing the entire block into one or two kernels to eliminate intermediate global memory traffic, with the main challenge being register pressure from the 16×128 MLP hidden dimension intermediate.
open_questions: What is the actual register usage for a fully-fused kernel holding 16×32 input + 16×96 QKV + 16×16 attention + 16×128 MLP intermediate in registers? Does it exceed the 255 register limit per thread?
Can tl.dot efficiently handle 16×32 × 32×N matmuls on RTX5090 tensor cores, or is the tile size too small for good utilization?
What is the optimal number of threads (BLOCK size / num_warps) per program for the fused kernel to balance register pressure vs occupancy?
Is the MLP phase better handled by tiling the hidden dimension (e.g., 32-wide chunks of fc1 output fed immediately into fc2 accumulation) to avoid materializing the full 16×128 intermediate?
How does L2 cache behavior affect weight reuse across 57600 programs accessing the same ~50KB of weight data simultaneously?
What is the reference implementation's actual latency on RTX5090 to establish the baseline for speedup measurement?
Does GELU approximation via tl.libdevice.tanh introduce numerical differences that could fail the correctness tolerance check?
For the two-kernel approach, does the extra 118MB intermediate traffic dominate over the register pressure savings?
